blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a compelling exploration of combining symbolic reasoning with deep learning, particularly in reinforcement learning. He emphasizes the intuitive appeal of learning representations and then performing higher-order reasoning on them, comparing it to how humans learn and form rules. The key insight is that such a hybrid system could be more data-efficient, interpretable, and capable of transfer learning compared to purely neural approaches. The paper proposes a prototype system that outperforms conventional deep reinforcement learning on a stochastic game variant by acquiring human-comprehensible symbolic rules. Colyer notes that this approach could bridge decades of AI research, addressing issues like brittleness, opacity, and the need for large training sets in modern DRL systems.
paper_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) brings the power of deep neural networks to bear on the generic task of trial-and-error learning, and its effectiveness has been convincingly demonstrated on tasks such as Atari video games and the game of Go. However, contemporary DRL systems inherit a number of shortcomings from the current generation of deep learning techniques. For example, they require very large datasets to work effectively, entailing that they are slow to learn even when such datasets are available. Moreover, they lack the ability to reason on an abstract level, which makes it difficult to implement high-level cognitive functions such as transfer learning, analogical reasoning, and hypothesis-based reasoning. Finally, their operation is largely opaque to humans, rendering them unsuitable for domains in which verifiability is important. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end reinforcement learning architecture comprising a neural back end and a symbolic front end with the potential to overcome each of these shortcomings. As proof-ofconcept, we present a preliminary implementation of the architecture and apply it to several variants of a simple video game. We show that the resulting system – though just a prototype – learns effectively, and, by acquiring a set of symbolic rules that are easily comprehensible to humans, dramatically outperforms a conventional, fully neural DRL system on a stochastic variant of the game.
